explanations.explanation: Verse 3 says the eagle “came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar.” Not a branch, not a few leaves, the top. He walked in like he owned the place, and I'm not sure he even looked around first.
The riddle never mentions a stone. The eagle “came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar.” An eagle hauling rocks would be a moving company, friend, and this is a riddle.
There's no flock anywhere in this riddle. Verse 3 says the eagle “took away the top of the cedar.” This eagle is after a tree, so the lambs can relax.

explanations.answer: In fertile soil by abundant waters
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 5 says the eagle “planted it in fertile soil” and “placed it by abundant waters.” Good dirt and plenty of water is about the best setup a plant can ask for.
The city of traders is where the cedar's topmost shoot went (verse 4). The seed of the land is a separate planting. Verse 5 says that seed went into fertile soil by abundant waters.

explanations.answer: On a high and lofty mountain
explanations.explanation: A high and lofty mountain does show up in this passage, but much later, in verse 22, and it's the LORD doing the planting there. The eagle's seed in verse 5 goes into fertile soil by abundant waters. Hold that mountain thought, friend.
Not quite. Verse 6 says the seed “sprouted and became a spreading vine, low in height.” A vine that spreads out low is nothing like a tower. Nobody's looking up at this thing.
Right, no tower here. Verse 6 says it “sprouted and became a spreading vine, low in height.” It spreads instead of standing tall.

explanations.answer: Toward the eagle who planted it
explanations.explanation: Verse 6 says the vine had “branches turned toward him.” The vine faces the eagle who planted it. It's keeping an eye on him the whole time.
Lebanon is where the cedar stood in verse 3, but the vine's branches aren't turned that way. Verse 6 says they're “turned toward him,” meaning the eagle. This vine only has eyes for one bird.
The text doesn't point the branches at any sun. Verse 6 says they were “turned toward him,” and the him is the eagle. Leave the sunflower work to the sunflowers.
Yes. Verse 7 says that when the second eagle appears, “this vine bent its roots toward him.” The vine leans toward him.
The text says the opposite. Verse 7 says “this vine bent its roots toward him,” meaning the second great eagle. It's not ignoring him.
Yes. Verse 7 says the vine stretched out its branches to him “so that he might water it.” Water is what it's reaching for.
Pruning means trimming, and the text never says that. The vine stretches out its branches so that he “might water it.” It wants a drink, friend, not a haircut.
Nobody is lifting anything in verse 7. The vine stretches out its branches “so that he might water it.” Water is the word you're looking for.

explanations.answer: It will be uprooted and wither
explanations.explanation: Right. God asks, “Will it not be uprooted and stripped of its fruit so that it shrivels?” and says, “All its foliage will wither!” (verse 9). The vine isn't going to come out of this well.

explanations.answer: It will grow into a cedar
explanations.explanation: A cedar isn't in the picture here. God asks whether the vine will flourish, then says it will be uprooted and its foliage will wither (verse 9). The cedar sprout doesn't show up until the end of the passage.

explanations.answer: It will bear a great harvest
explanations.explanation: The opposite, friend. God says the vine will be “stripped of its fruit so that it shrivels” (verse 9). There's no harvest in this vine's future.
God says the reverse. Verse 9 says, “It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it up by its roots.” No heavy lifting required.
Right. Verse 9 says, “It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it up by its roots.” One good tug and it's done.
Yes. Verse 10 asks, “Will it not completely wither when the east wind strikes?” Even if the vine moves somewhere new, that wind is still coming.
The text doesn't mention summer heat. Verse 10 says the vine will wither “when the east wind strikes.” Wind is the one doing the striking.
There's no bug trouble in this riddle. Verse 10 says the vine will “completely wither when the east wind strikes.” The east wind is the answer, and no locusts were invited.
Yes. Verse 12 says, “the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, carried off its king and officials, and brought them back with him to Babylon.” The riddle's first eagle now has a real name.
The text doesn't name Aram. Verse 12 says it was “the king of Babylon” who came to Jerusalem and carried off its king and officials. He took them back with him to Babylon.
Moab isn't in this explanation. Verse 12 names “the king of Babylon,” who came to Jerusalem and carried off its king and officials.

explanations.answer: Makes a covenant with him under oath
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 13 says the king of Babylon “made a covenant with him, putting him under oath.” An oath is a serious promise, and this one has a covenant behind it.

explanations.answer: Makes him a servant in his palace
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't put him in a palace job. Verse 13 says the king of Babylon “made a covenant with him, putting him under oath.” It's a promise, not a job.

explanations.answer: Puts him in chains in the city
explanations.explanation: No chains here. Verse 13 says the king of Babylon “made a covenant with him, putting him under oath.” That's an oath, not a prison sentence.

The text says the opposite. Verse 14 says the leading men were carried away “so that the kingdom would be brought low, unable to lift itself up, surviving only by keeping his covenant.” The kingdom isn't built to stand alone.
Right. Verse 14 says it was “so that the kingdom would be brought low, unable to lift itself up, surviving only by keeping his covenant.” That's a kingdom with no way to stand on its own.
Yes. Verse 15 says this king rebelled “by sending his envoys to Egypt.” An envoy is someone sent to carry a message.
Assyria isn't the place. Verse 15 says the king rebelled “by sending his envoys to Egypt.” That's where the messengers went.
The text doesn't name Edom. Verse 15 says he sent his envoys “to Egypt.” They're headed there, not to Edom.
Yes. Verse 15 says the king sent envoys to Egypt “to ask for horses and a large army.” He's shopping for muscle.
Grain isn't on this shopping list. Verse 15 says he sent envoys to Egypt “to ask for horses and a large army.” That's a military request.
The text doesn't mention builders. Verse 15 says the request was “for horses and a large army.” He's asking for fighters, not a work crew.

Yes. In verse 16, God declares that “he will die in Babylon, in the land of the king who enthroned him, whose oath he despised and whose covenant he broke.” He doesn't escape the king he rebelled against.
That's what God says. Verse 16 has the Lord GOD declaring, “…he will die in Babylon, in the land of the king who enthroned him…” The king who broke his oath ends up in Babylon.

God says the reverse. Verse 17 says, “Pharaoh with his mighty army and vast horde will not help him in battle.” Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, the one this king sent his envoys to. The help he asked for doesn't come.

Right. Verse 17 says, “Pharaoh with his mighty army and vast horde will not help him in battle.” Pharaoh, king of Egypt, has the army, and it doesn't show up. A big army is no help when it never arrives.

explanations.answer: The treason he committed against God
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says He will “execute judgment upon him there for the treason he committed against Me” (verse 20). The text names this as the reason.

explanations.answer: The raids he made on Babylon
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention raids. Verse 20 says the judgment is “for the treason he committed against Me.” The treason is against God.

explanations.answer: The gold he took from the temple
explanations.explanation: No stolen gold is in this passage. Verse 20 says God will execute judgment “for the treason he committed against Me.” That's the charge.

explanations.answer: They are scattered to every wind
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 21 says, “those who survive will be scattered to every wind.” They're blown in every direction like crumbs off a cookie sheet.

explanations.answer: They are hidden in the hills
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't tuck them away anywhere. Verse 21 says “those who survive will be scattered to every wind.” They're scattered, not hidden.

explanations.answer: They are sent home to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No trip home is described here. Verse 21 says “those who survive will be scattered to every wind.” They get scattered.
Yes. In verse 22 the Lord GOD says, “I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out.” The one who does the taking this time is God.
Ezekiel is the one speaking God's words, but the "I" in verse 22 is the Lord GOD. He says, “I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out.” Ezekiel doesn't take it.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was the one who wasn't going to help in battle (verse 17). In verse 22 the Lord GOD says, “I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out.” Pharaoh isn't part of this planting.

explanations.answer: On the mountain heights of Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches” (verse 23). It's planted in Israel's high places.

The city of traders is where the eagle planted the shoot back in verse 4. In verse 23 the LORD says, “I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel.” It's a different planting in a different place.
The text doesn't plant it by any rivers. In verse 23 the LORD says, “I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel.” The planting is in Israel.
Yes. Verse 23 says it will “bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar.” The little sprig grows into a cedar.
The vine was the eagle's planting back in verses 5 and 6. In verse 23 the LORD's sprig becomes “a majestic cedar.” That's a different plant and a much grander one.
A willow is what the eagle set the seed out like (verse 5). The LORD's sprig in verse 23 becomes “a majestic cedar.” A willow doesn't make the cut here.
The text says more than that. Verse 23 says, “Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches.” That's every kind of bird, with plenty of shade for all of them.
Right. Verse 23 says, “Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches.” Every kind of bird is welcome.
Yes. Verse 24 says, “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.” The tall one comes down and the low one goes up.
God doesn't cut the low tree down. Verse 24 says, “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.” The low tree gets lifted.
The low tree doesn't stay low. In verse 24 God says, “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.” This is a promotion for the little tree.
Yes. Verse 24 says, “I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish.” God dries up the green one, and the withered one gets to flourish.
God does say it. Verse 24 says, “I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish.” The green tree dries up, and the withered one flourishes.
